claim: The dataset contains 459 layer II neurons from nine separate recordings in five mice.
source: Our dataset contains 459 layer II neurons from nine separate recordings in five mice (Figure 1C; 33–73 well-isolated units per recording, see Methods and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–E).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of neurons, recordings, and mice in the dataset.

claim: In a subset of experiments (6/9), simultaneous recordings were obtained from olfactory bulb cells (126 neurons from ventrolateral mitral cell layer).
source: In a subset of these experiments (6/9) we obtained simultaneous recordings from olfactory bulb cells (126 neurons from ventrolateral mitral cell layer, see Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of experiments with simultaneous bulb recordings and the number of neurons recorded.

claim: Piriform cortex cells typically had low spontaneous firing rates with a log-normal distribution (mean: 3.09 Hz; median: 1.68 Hz; st. dev: 3.93 Hz; range: 0.0028–40.8 Hz).
source: Piriform cortex cells typically had low spontaneous firing rates with a log-normal distribution (mean: 3.09 Hz; median: 1.68 Hz; st. dev: 3.93 Hz; range: 0.0028–40.8 Hz; Figure 1—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific statistical measures of spontaneous firing rates and references a figure showing the distribution.

claim: Individual cells exhibited weak phase preferences that were uniformly distributed across the sniff so that population spiking was decoupled from respiration.
source: Individual cells exhibited weak phase preferences that were uniformly distributed across the sniff so that, unlike in anesthetized conditions (Rennaker et al., 2007; Poo and Isaacson, 2009), population spiking was decoupled from respiration (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The manuscript describes the phase preference distribution and contrasts it with anesthetized conditions, citing prior work.

claim: Approximately 93% of the recorded units were principal neurons.
source: We estimate that ~93% of these units were principal neurons (see Figure 9), which is consistent with histological measures (Suzuki and Bekkers, 2010).
evidence: The manuscript provides an estimate based on data shown in Figure 9 and cites a histological study for consistency.

claim: Respiration barely changed during odor presentation, indicating that odor-evoked changes in neural activity were not complicated by changes in sniffing.
source: While animals typically sniffed actively after odor offset (Figure 1D), respiration barely changed during the odor presentation (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), indicating that odor-evoked changes we observed in neural activity were not complicated by changes in sniffing.
evidence: The manuscript describes respiration patterns during odor presentation and references supporting figures.

claim: Using a strict criterion, 23% of cells (105/459 cells) were activated by at least one of the six odors.
source: Using this strict criterion, 23% of cells (105/459 cells) were activated by at least one of the six odors, while 33% of cells (150/459 cells) were suppressed, and on average, each odor activated and suppressed 6.7% and 13.3% of cells, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and cell counts based on statistical criteria.

claim: 33% of cells (150/459 cells) were suppressed by at least one of the six odors.
source: Using this strict criterion, 23% of cells (105/459 cells) were activated by at least one of the six odors, while 33% of cells (150/459 cells) were suppressed, and on average, each odor activated and suppressed 6.7% and 13.3% of cells, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and cell counts based on statistical criteria.

claim: On average, each odor activated 6.7% of cells and suppressed 13.3% of cells.
source: Using this strict criterion, 23% of cells (105/459 cells) were activated by at least one of the six odors, while 33% of cells (150/459 cells) were suppressed, and on average, each odor activated and suppressed 6.7% and 13.3% of cells, respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages based on statistical analysis.

claim: Trial-to-trial correlations within repeated presentations of the same odorant were 0.48 ± 0.12.
source: To quantify that we computed correlations between single-trial response vectors for repeated presentations of the same odorant (0.48 ± 0.12; n = 6 odors, 9 recordings).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific correlation values with statistical measures.

claim: Inter-odorant responses were significantly lower than within-odorant correlations but nevertheless much higher than expected by chance (0.38 ± 0.09, p<0.001).
source: We then compared these to responses to different odors. Inter-odorant responses were significantly lower, but nevertheless much higher than expected by chance (0.38 ± 0.09, p<0.001, paired t-test).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific correlation values with statistical significance testing.

claim: Only 4% of cells (18/459 cells) showed mixed responses (both activation and suppression to different odors).
source: Moreover, only 4% of cells (18/459 cells) showed mixed responses, whereas the distribution of mixed responses predicted from independent ensembles would be 14% (66/459; Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific cell counts and percentages compared to a predicted distribution.

claim: The distribution of mixed responses predicted from independent ensembles would be 14% (66/459).
source: Moreover, only 4% of cells (18/459 cells) showed mixed responses, whereas the distribution of mixed responses predicted from independent ensembles would be 14% (66/459; Figure 1J, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: The manuscript provides a predicted distribution based on a model of independent ensembles.

claim: There are functionally distinct subclasses of piriform neurons that encode odor stimuli exclusively through either activation or suppression.
source: Our data therefore suggest that there are functionally distinct subclasses of piriform neurons that encode odor stimuli exclusively through either activation or suppression, consistent with a recent imaging study (Otazu et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the data on response polarity and cites a supporting study.

claim: Trial-to-trial correlations within and across stimuli were lower in piriform cortex than in olfactory bulb.
source: Trial-to-trial correlations within and across stimuli were lower in piriform cortex than in olfactory bulb (Figure 2B).
evidence: The manuscript compares correlation values between the two brain regions and references a figure.

claim: Correlations in both olfactory bulb and piriform cortex decreased systematically with differences in concentration, becoming as dissimilar over a 30-fold concentration range as responses to two different odorants.
source: Notably, correlations in both olfactory bulb and piriform cortex decreased systematically with differences in concentration, becoming as dissimilar over a 30-fold concentration range as responses to two different odorants.
evidence: The manuscript describes a systematic relationship between concentration differences and correlation values.

claim: Odor representations in both olfactory bulb and piriform cortex, defined by spike counts, are not concentration invariant.
source: This analysis reveals that odor representations in both olfactory bulb and piriform cortex, defined by spike counts, are not concentration invariant.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the correlation analysis across concentrations.

claim: Total spiking output from olfactory bulb remained unchanged across concentrations (0.1-1%).
source: However total bulb spiking remained unchanged across concentrations (Figure 2C), indicating that substantial normalization occurs in olfactory bulb, consistent with recent imaging (Banerjee et al., 2015; Economo et al., 2016; Roland et al., 2016) and electrophysiology (Sirotin et al., 2015) studies.
evidence: The manuscript reports no significant change in total spiking and cites supporting studies.

claim: Substantial normalization occurs in olfactory bulb.
source: However total bulb spiking remained unchanged across concentrations (Figure 2C), indicating that substantial normalization occurs in olfactory bulb, consistent with recent imaging (Banerjee et al., 2015; Economo et al., 2016; Roland et al., 2016) and electrophysiology (Sirotin et al., 2015) studies.
evidence: The manuscript infers normalization from the unchanged total spiking and cites supporting studies.

claim: Total spiking in piriform cortex decreased slightly at higher concentrations.
source: Interestingly, total spiking in piriform cortex decreased slightly at higher concentrations (Figure 2C).
evidence: The manuscript reports a slight decrease in total spiking with concentration.

claim: The number of activated neurons did not change with concentration in piriform cortex.
source: First, the number of activated neurons did not change with concentration, although more cells were suppressed at higher concentrations (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports no significant change in the number of activated neurons across concentrations.

claim: More cells were suppressed at higher concentrations in piriform cortex.
source: First, the number of activated neurons did not change with concentration, although more cells were suppressed at higher concentrations (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports a significant increase in suppressed cells with concentration.

claim: Spiking in individual activated cells showed no systematic relationship to odorant concentration.
source: Second, spiking in individual activated cells showed no systematic relationship to odorant concentration, although, again, suppression was weakly concentration-dependent (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports no systematic relationship between spike counts and concentration for activated cells.

claim: Suppression was weakly concentration-dependent in piriform cortex.
source: Second, spiking in individual activated cells showed no systematic relationship to odorant concentration, although, again, suppression was weakly concentration-dependent (Figure 2E).
evidence: The manuscript reports a weak concentration-dependence for suppression.

claim: A simple rate code cannot be used to represent odor intensity in piriform cortex.
source: Therefore, a simple rate code cannot be used to represent odor intensity in piriform cortex.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the lack of systematic spike count changes with concentration.

claim: Population spiking peaked within 50-100 ms after inhalation.
source: Averaging across all experiments (Figure 3B), we again found a rapid increase in spiking that occurred within 50–100 ms after inhalation.
evidence: The manuscript describes the timing of the peak in population spiking.

claim: The peak of population spiking increased slightly at higher concentrations (0.03%: 4.39 Hz ±1.33 Hz; 1%: 5.14 Hz ±2.16 Hz; p=0.0159).
source: This peak increased slightly at higher concentrations (0.03% mean ± st. dev.: 4.39 Hz ±1.33 Hz; 1%: 5.14 Hz ±2.16 Hz; repeated measures ANOVA, F(3, 51)=3.78, p=0.0159, n = 18).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific values and statistical testing for the peak increase.

claim: There is a systematic, concentration-dependent redistribution of spike times in piriform cortex.
source: This small increase in peak spiking, together with the small decrease in total spiking, indicates that there is a systematic, concentration-dependent redistribution of spike times (Figure 3C).
evidence: The manuscript infers redistribution from the changes in peak and total spiking.

claim: Response latencies decreased systematically at higher concentrations across the population.
source: Across the population, we found a systematic concentration-dependent decrease in response latency (Figure 4B).
evidence: The manuscript reports a systematic decrease in latencies with concentration.

claim: The earliest responses were largely concentration-invariant.
source: However, the earliest responses were largely concentration-invariant, and concentration-dependent effects were greatest for cells that responded >100 ms later, suggesting again that there are functionally distinct classes of responses.
evidence: The manuscript describes the concentration-invariance of early responses based on latency analysis.

claim: Concentration-dependent effects were greatest for cells that responded >100 ms later.
source: However, the earliest responses were largely concentration-invariant, and concentration-dependent effects were greatest for cells that responded >100 ms later, suggesting again that there are functionally distinct classes of responses.
evidence: The manuscript describes the timing of concentration-dependent effects.

claim: The distributions of response latencies at all four concentrations were well fit by a mixture of Gaussian functions.
source: In fact, the distributions of response latencies at all four concentrations were well fit by a mixture of Gaussian functions (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the fitting of latency distributions with Gaussian mixtures.

claim: Time to peak of the first Gaussian barely changed across concentrations.
source: Time to peak of the first Gaussian barely changed across concentrations while the peak of the second Gaussian shifted systematically from 206 ms at 0.03% to 136 ms at 1% (Figure 4F).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific timing values from Gaussian fits.

claim: The peak of the second Gaussian shifted systematically from 206 ms at 0.03% to 136 ms at 1%.
source: Time to peak of the first Gaussian barely changed across concentrations while the peak of the second Gaussian shifted systematically from 206 ms at 0.03% to 136 ms at 1% (Figure 4F).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific timing values from Gaussian fits.

claim: The cortical odor response is composed of two phases that become more synchronous at higher concentrations.
source: Thus, the cortical odor response is composed of two phases that become more synchronous at higher concentrations.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the Gaussian mixture analysis.

claim: Odor identity can be decoded simply by knowing which cells respond, with no additional information provided by spike count, spike time, or odor-evoked suppression.
source: In support of this model we find that odor identity can be decoded simply by knowing which cells respond (Figure 4B,E). Interestingly, information about spike count, spike time and odor-evoked suppression appear redundant for identity coding.
evidence: The manuscript reports decoding results showing that binary membership codes are sufficient for identity.

claim: Accurate and efficient odor intensity decoding requires information about spike times but is not improved by knowing spike counts.
source: By contrast, accurate and efficient odor intensity decoding requires information about spike times but is not improved by knowing spike counts (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports decoding results showing that binned spike counts improve intensity decoding over summed counts.

claim: Odorant classification accuracy reached 90% with 145 cells using membership code, 115 cells using summed spike count, and 75 cells using binned spike count.
source: Odorant classification accuracy, averaged across pseudopopulations, quickly rose using all three types of response vectors (mean number of cells to reach 90% accuracy: membership, 145 cells; summed, 115 cells; binned, 75 cells; Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific cell numbers required to reach 90% accuracy for different coding schemes.

claim: Differences in classifier performance using different coding schemes did not reach statistical significance for odorant classification.
source: However, differences in classifier performance with the same sets of cells using any of the three different coding schemes did not reach statistical significance over any tested population sizes (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical testing of differences between coding schemes.

claim: Concentration classification was less accurate than classification of different odorants.
source: In general, concentration classification was less accurate than classification of different odorants.
evidence: The manuscript compares classification accuracy between tasks.

claim: Concentration classification using binary response vectors did not reach 90% accuracy.
source: Classifier performance using binary response vectors as inputs was relatively poor and did not reach the 90% accuracy criterion.
evidence: The manuscript reports that binary codes were insufficient for accurate concentration decoding.

claim: Concentration classification accuracy only improved marginally when using spike count vectors (90% accuracy with 425 cells).
source: Classification accuracy only improved marginally when using spike count vectors (90% accuracy with 425 cells; Figure 5—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific cell numbers required for 90% accuracy with spike count vectors.

claim: Classification accuracy and efficiency increased significantly using binned response vectors for concentration (90% accuracy with 210 cells).
source: However, if spike time information is used to represent odor intensity then using binned response vectors should improve classification. Indeed, classification accuracy and efficiency increased significantly using binned response vectors (90% accuracy with 210 cells; Figure 5—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific cell numbers and statistical significance for binned vector performance.

claim: Spike time information provides more information about odor concentration than spike count.
source: Thus, we conclude that spike time information provides more information about odor concentration than spike count.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the decoding analysis comparing different coding schemes.

claim: Lifetime sparseness for piriform neurons was 0.34 ± 0.21 (n = 459 cells).
source: However, our measures of both lifetime sparseness (0.34 ± 0.21; n = 459 cells); Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and population sparseness (0.68 ± 0.10, n = 54 population-odors) in awake, head-fixed mice are considerably lower than in urethane-anesthetized rats (Poo and Isaacson, 2009) and slightly lower than in trained rats performing an odor-discrimination task (Miura et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific sparseness values and compares them to prior studies.

claim: Population sparseness for piriform neurons was 0.68 ± 0.10 (n = 54 population-odors).
source: However, our measures of both lifetime sparseness (0.34 ± 0.21; n = 459 cells); Figure 1—figure supplement 2) and population sparseness (0.68 ± 0.10, n = 54 population-odors) in awake, head-fixed mice are considerably lower than in urethane-anesthetized rats (Poo and Isaacson, 2009) and slightly lower than in trained rats performing an odor-discrimination task (Miura et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific sparseness values and compares them to prior studies.

claim: Randomly selected subpopulations of only 10 neurons had an average accuracy of >50% for odorant classification.
source: First, the range of performances is small. Randomly selected subpopulations of only 10 neurons had an average accuracy of >50%.
evidence: The manuscript reports classification accuracy for small random populations.

claim: Accuracy was above chance 98% of the time for populations of 10 neurons.
source: Importantly, accuracy was above chance 98% of the time for this population size (Figure 5B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the frequency of above-chance performance for small populations.

claim: The distribution of classifier performances were normally distributed when classifying different odorants, concentrations, or generalizing for odor identity using subpopulations of 25 cells.
source: Instead, we found the distribution of performances were normally distributed when classifying different odorants (Figure 5B), concentrations (Figure 5C), or generalizing for odor identity (Figure 5E), using any of the decoding strategies.
evidence: The manuscript describes the distribution of classifier performances for small populations.

claim: Cortical odor representations are not especially sparse.
source: We therefore conclude that cortical odor representations are not especially sparse.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the decoding analysis and sparseness measures.

claim: Odor identity could be accurately classified within ~100 ms after inhalation.
source: Using an expanding window as input (Figure 6A), we could accurately classify the odorant and generalize for odor identity within ~100 ms after inhalation (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript reports the time required for accurate identity classification.

claim: Intensity decoding accuracy remained poor during the initial ~100 ms and then increased steadily over the next ~100 ms.
source: However, intensity decoding accuracy remained poor during the initial ~100 ms and then increased steadily over the next ~100 ms.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal evolution of intensity decoding accuracy.

claim: The earliest inputs generate a concentration-invariant representation of odor identity and odor intensity is encoded by the relative timing of later responses.
source: This result supports a model in which the earliest inputs generate a concentration-invariant representation of odor identity and odor intensity is encoded by the relative timing of later responses.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this model based on the temporal decoding analysis.

claim: As concentration decoding improved, the ability to generalize across concentrations decreased.
source: However, as concentration decoding improved, the ability to generalize across concentrations decreased (Figure 6D), consistent with a trade-off between a concentration-invariant representation of odor identity and a representation of odor intensity.
evidence: The manuscript reports the temporal trade-off between identity and intensity decoding.

claim: Trained mice take longer to discriminate differences in odor concentrations than they require to discriminate distinct odors.
source: Interestingly, trained mice take longer to discriminate differences in odor concentrations than they require to discriminate distinct odors (Abraham et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript cites a behavioral study showing differences in discrimination times.

claim: The differences in the amount of time required to represent identity vs. intensity could underlie the difference in reaction times for discriminating odors vs. concentrations.
source: The differences we find in the amount of time required to represent identity vs. intensity could underlie, at least in part, this difference in reaction times.
evidence: The manuscript proposes a link between neural coding dynamics and behavioral reaction times.

claim: The distribution of bulb response latencies was well fit with a mixture of Gaussians.
source: As in piriform, the distribution of bulb response latencies was well fit with a mixture of Gaussians (Figure 7 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript describes the fitting of bulb latency distributions.

claim: Latencies of the first responses in olfactory bulb were rapid and barely changed with concentration.
source: Latencies of the first responses were rapid and barely changed with concentration.
evidence: The manuscript describes the concentration-invariance of early bulb responses.

claim: Fast bulb responses overlapped with the first phase of piriform responses.
source: These fast bulb responses overlapped with the first phase of piriform responses (Figure 7D), consistent with the earliest activated cells in bulb driving the fast responses in piriform.
evidence: The manuscript compares timing of bulb and piriform responses and infers a causal relationship.

claim: Latencies of the second peak in olfactory bulb responses decreased with concentration.
source: Again like piriform, latencies of the second peak in olfactory bulb responses decreased with concentration (Figure 7—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript describes concentration-dependent changes in bulb response timing.

claim: At low concentrations (0.03%), the second peak appeared to occur earlier in bulb (192 ms) than piriform cortex (206 ms).
source: At low concentrations (0.03%) this peak appeared to occur earlier in bulb (192 ms) than piriform cortex (206 ms).
evidence: The manuscript compares timing of the second peak between bulb and piriform at low concentrations.

claim: At high concentrations (1%), the second phase appeared to peak earlier in piriform (136 ms) than bulb (151 ms), although bootstrapped confidence intervals overlapped.
source: However, interestingly, the second phase appeared to peak earlier in piriform (136 ms) than bulb (151 ms) at high concentrations (1%), although bootstrapped confidence intervals for the timing of these peaks overlapped.
evidence: The manuscript compares timing of the second peak between bulb and piriform at high concentrations with statistical uncertainty.

claim: The second phase of responses is more prominent in bulb than in piriform cortex at all but the highest concentration.
source: At all concentrations, the early peak in the bulb response aligned with the early peak in the piriform response (Figure 8A). However, the second phase of the response was much more pronounced in bulb than piriform, indicating that later bulb input is actively suppressed within piriform cortex.
evidence: The manuscript compares the prominence of the second phase between bulb and piriform and infers active suppression.

claim: Later bulb input is actively suppressed within piriform cortex.
source: However, the second phase of the response was much more pronounced in bulb than piriform, indicating that later bulb input is actively suppressed within piriform cortex.
evidence: The manuscript infers active suppression from the difference in second phase prominence.

claim: Piriform cortex is preferentially responsive to the earliest-active bulb inputs.
source: This result suggests that although individual mitral/tufted cells may fire at different phases throughout the sniff cycle (Bathellier et al., 2008; Cury and Uchida, 2010; Shusterman et al., 2011) piriform cortex is preferentially responsive to the earliest-active bulb inputs.
evidence: The manuscript infers preferential responsiveness from the suppression of later inputs and cites supporting studies.

claim: The shift in response latencies is more pronounced in piriform cortex than in olfactory bulb.
source: While latencies decreased systematically with concentration in both structures, both latency to first spike and latency to peak were more steeply concentration-dependent in piriform cortex (Figure 8D,E).
evidence: The manuscript compares the steepness of concentration-dependent latency changes between bulb and piriform.

claim: There is an active transformation of bulb input within piriform cortex in which later inputs from bulb are suppressed and the population response is temporally sharpened with concentration.
source: Together, these data indicate an active transformation of bulb input within piriform cortex in which later inputs from bulb are suppressed and the population response is temporally sharpened with concentration.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the comparison of bulb and piriform response dynamics.

claim: Approximately 7% of cells (35/512) exhibited robust and sustained light-evoked spiking and were identified as inhibitory interneurons.
source: While light pulses suppressed spontaneous spiking in most neurons, ~7% of cells (35/512, n = 9 recordings) exhibited robust and sustained light-evoked spiking (Figure 9C). We concluded that these cells were ChR2+ and defined them as inhibitory interneurons.
evidence: The manuscript reports the percentage of cells identified as inhibitory based on optogenetic responses.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons responded to most odors with an increase in spiking (lifetime sparseness: 0.11).
source: Thus identified, inhibitory interneurons responded to most odors with an increase in spiking (lifetime sparseness: 0.11; Figure 9D–F).
evidence: The manuscript reports the response properties and sparseness of identified inhibitory neurons.

claim: The broadly tuned activation of inhibitory cells is consistent with the widespread suppression observed across the population.
source: This broadly tuned activation of inhibitory cells is consistent with the widespread suppression we observe across the population (Figure 1I).
evidence: The manuscript links the properties of inhibitory neurons to population-level suppression.

claim: Inhibitory population PSTHs revealed a sharp peak that rapidly decayed and then sustained at a lower level for the duration of the sniff.
source: These revealed a sharp peak that rapidly decayed and then sustained at a lower level for the duration of the sniff.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal profile of inhibitory population activity.

claim: The peak amplitude of the inhibitory PSTH increased systematically with concentration.
source: The peak amplitude of the PSTH increased systematically with concentration.
evidence: The manuscript reports concentration-dependent changes in inhibitory activity.

claim: Onset time of inhibition was ~25 ms at all concentrations.
source: Onset time was ~25 ms at all concentrations.
evidence: The manuscript reports the concentration-invariance of inhibition onset.

claim: Latency to peak of inhibition decreased from 91 ms at 0.03% to 65 ms at 1%.
source: However, latency to peak decreased (0.03%, 91 ms; 1%, 65 ms) and the initial peak became narrower (FWHM: 0.03%, 89 ms; 1%, 50 ms), indicating that cortical inhibition occurs earlier and sharpens at higher concentrations.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific timing values for inhibition at different concentrations.

claim: The initial peak of inhibition became narrower at higher concentrations (FWHM: 0.03%, 89 ms; 1%, 50 ms).
source: However, latency to peak decreased (0.03%, 91 ms; 1%, 65 ms) and the initial peak became narrower (FWHM: 0.03%, 89 ms; 1%, 50 ms), indicating that cortical inhibition occurs earlier and sharpens at higher concentrations.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific width values for inhibition at different concentrations.

claim: Cortical inhibition occurs earlier and sharpens at higher concentrations.
source: However, latency to peak decreased (0.03%, 91 ms; 1%, 65 ms) and the initial peak became narrower (FWHM: 0.03%, 89 ms; 1%, 50 ms), indicating that cortical inhibition occurs earlier and sharpens at higher concentrations.
evidence: The manuscript draws this conclusion from the timing and width measurements of inhibition.

claim: The first peak of the population response immediately preceded the increase in inhibition.
source: The first peak of the population response immediately preceded the increase in inhibition.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal relationship between excitation and inhibition.

claim: The second phase of the population response occurs immediately after the initial, sharp increase in inhibition has ended.
source: Importantly, the second phase of the population response, whose timing changes with concentration, occurs immediately after the initial, sharp increase in inhibition has ended.
evidence: The manuscript describes the temporal relationship between the second phase of excitation and inhibition.

claim: The onset of the second phase of the population response is shaped by intracortical inhibition.
source: This suggests that the onset of the second phase of the population response is shaped by intracortical inhibition.
evidence: The manuscript infers that inhibition shapes the second phase based on temporal relationships.

claim: Odor identity and odor intensity are represented using distinct and non-interfering coding strategies in piriform cortex.
source: We therefore propose that odor identity and odor intensity are represented using distinct and non-interfering coding strategies in piriform cortex.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this model based on the decoding analyses showing different optimal coding schemes for identity and intensity.

claim: Olfactory sensory neurons expressing a given receptor project to a unique pair of glomeruli in the olfactory bulb.
source: Each olfactory sensory neuron expresses just one type of odorant receptor, and all sensory neurons expressing a given receptor project to a unique pair of glomeruli in the olfactory bulb, so that odors are first represented by combinations of active glomeruli that each represent elemental molecular features of the odorant (Wilson and Mainen, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript describes the organization of olfactory sensory neuron projections and cites a supporting reference.

claim: Odors are first represented by combinations of active glomeruli that each represent elemental molecular features of the odorant.
source: Each olfactory sensory neuron expresses just one type of odorant receptor, and all sensory neurons expressing a given receptor project to a unique pair of glomeruli in the olfactory bulb, so that odors are first represented by combinations of active glomeruli that each represent elemental molecular features of the odorant (Wilson and Mainen, 2006).
evidence: The manuscript describes the combinatorial coding of odors in the olfactory bulb and cites a supporting reference.

claim: Piriform cortex is thought to give rise to the perception of 'odor objects' that represent different features of the odor, including its identity and intensity.
source: This information is then projected by olfactory bulb mitral/tufted cells to piriform cortex, where it is integrated and synthesized, and thought to give rise to the perception of 'odor objects' that should represent different features of the odor, including its identity and intensity (Gottfried, 2010; Wilson and Sullivan, 2011).
evidence: The manuscript describes the proposed function of piriform cortex and cites supporting references.

claim: Odors activate distributed and overlapping ensembles of piriform neurons, with a small fraction of cells responding strongly to any given stimulus.
source: Odors activate distributed and overlapping ensembles of piriform neurons, with a small fraction of cells responding strongly to any given stimulus (Illig and Haberly, 2003; Rennaker et al., 2007; Poo and Isaacson, 2009; Stettler and Axel, 2009).
evidence: The manuscript describes the response properties of piriform neurons and cites multiple supporting studies.

claim: Different odorants can be accurately decoded from populations of piriform neurons using spike counts across the population (i.e. a rate code), with little additional information provided by spike time.
source: Studies in awake, behaving rodents have shown that different odorants can be accurately decoded from populations of piriform neurons using spike counts across the population (i.e. a rate code), with little additional information provided by spike time (Miura et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites a prior study showing rate coding in piriform cortex.

claim: Input to olfactory bulb glomeruli is strongly concentration-dependent.
source: While input to olfactory bulb glomeruli is strongly concentration-dependent (Rubin and Katz, 1999; Spors and Grinvald, 2002), olfactory bulb output may be normalized over a large range of concentrations (Banerjee et al., 2015; Sirotin et al., 2015; Economo et al., 2016; Roland et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior studies showing concentration-dependent glomerular input.

claim: Olfactory bulb output may be normalized over a large range of concentrations.
source: While input to olfactory bulb glomeruli is strongly concentration-dependent (Rubin and Katz, 1999; Spors and Grinvald, 2002), olfactory bulb output may be normalized over a large range of concentrations (Banerjee et al., 2015; Sirotin et al., 2015; Economo et al., 2016; Roland et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites recent studies suggesting normalization in olfactory bulb output.

claim: Odors typically retain their perceptual identities across a range of concentrations.
source: Odors typically retain their perceptual identities across a range of concentrations (Krone et al., 2001; Laing et al., 2003; Homma et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites behavioral studies showing concentration-invariant odor perception.

claim: No previous studies have attempted to decode odor concentration from neural activity in piriform cortex.
source: No previous studies have attempted to decode odor concentration from neural activity in piriform cortex.
evidence: The manuscript states that this is a novel analysis.

claim: Odors activate different olfactory bulb glomeruli and mitral/tufted cells at specific phases of the respiration cycle.
source: Odors activate different olfactory bulb glomeruli and mitral/tufted cells at specific phases of the respiration cycle (Spors et al., 2006; Bathellier et al., 2008; Cury and Uchida, 2010; Shusterman et al., 2011).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies showing respiration-locked responses in olfactory bulb.

claim: Increasing odorant concentration typically does not increase spiking systematically in responsive mitral/tufted cells, but rather decreases their onset latencies.
source: Increasing odorant concentration typically does not increase spiking systematically in responsive mitral/tufted cells, but rather decreases their onset latencies (Chalansonnet and Chaput, 1998; Cang and Isaacson, 2003; Margrie and Schaefer, 2003; Fukunaga et al., 2012; Sirotin et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites multiple studies showing latency-based concentration coding in olfactory bulb.

claim: The same subset of mitral/tufted cells may be activated by a given odorant at different concentrations, but with shorter latencies at higher concentrations.
source: Therefore, the same subset of mitral/tufted cells may be activated by a given odorant at different concentrations, but with shorter latencies at higher concentrations.
evidence: The manuscript infers this from cited studies on concentration-dependent latencies.

claim: If different features of the piriform response are sensitive to the spatial and the temporal patterns of its input from olfactory bulb, then these features could independently represent odor identity and odor intensity.
source: Thus, if different features of the piriform response are sensitive to the spatial and the temporal (Haddad et al., 2013) patterns of its input from olfactory bulb, then these features could independently represent odor identity and odor intensity.
evidence: The manuscript proposes this hypothesis based on the properties of bulb input and cites a supporting study.

claim: Olfactory bulb projections to piriform cortex show no discernible topography.
